## Open Science in the world

**The Open Science by UNESCO**

> Open science aims at making scientific knowledge openly available, accessible and reusable. The key elements of open science include: open access to scientific knowledge (including open access to scientific publications, data, educational resources, software and hardware); open infrastructures; open engagement with society and dialogue with indigenous and traditional knowledge systems, among others[^UNESCO].

[^UNESCO]: [UNESCO](https://www.unesco.org/en/open-science)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-unesco-logo.png){width=80%}
:::

::: {.column width=70%}

UNESCO asks member States to :

**1.** Promote a shared understanding of open science and set out diverse paths to achieving it<br>
**2.** Develop an enabling policy environment for open science<br>
**3.** Invest in infrastructure and activities that contribute to open science<br>
**4.** Invest in training, education, digital literacy and capacity-building to support open science<br>
**5.** Foster a culture of open science and align incentives to support it<br>
**6.** Promote innovative approaches for open science at all stages of the scientific process<br>
**7.** Encourage international and multi-stakeholder cooperation in the context of open science to reduce gaps in technology and knowledge<br>
:::

::::

## Open Science in Europe

> The ambition of the **European Open Science Cloud**, known as EOSC, is to develop a **Web of FAIR Data and Services** for science in Europe. The implementation of EOSC is based on a long-term process of alignment and coordination pursued by the Commission since 2015.[^EOSC].

[^EOSC]: [EOSC](https://eosc.eu/)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-eosc-logo.png){width=80%}
:::

::: {.column width=70%}

EOSC will also improve the situation for researchers in many ways, namely by :

**1.** Enhancing scientific research by providing access to a weath of data and research outputs from various fields and institutions.<br>
**2.** Fostering innovation by making it easier for researchers to share, collaborate and build on each others’ work.<br>
**3.** Improving transparency and reproducibility of research by making data and methods more open and accessible<br>
**4.** Reducing data silos and duplication of efforts by promoting data sharing and reuse<br>
**5.** Facilitating interdisciplinarity research and cross-sectoral collaboration by making data and resources from different domains more easily available<br>
:::

::::

## Open Science in France

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
**Missions**

- To ensure the coordinated implementation, with higher education and research institutions, of the national open science strategy
- To enable the development of open science skills within the scientific community
- To coordinate France's actions in the field of open science at the European and international level
- Define the principles and guidelines for the use of funds from the National Open Science Fund
- Define the principles and guidelines for negotiations with the main publishers of scientific publications 
- To propose to the ministers responsible for research and higher education and to public authorities all actions likely to strengthen or promote access to knowledge, data, software and source code for research

## Open Science in France

**Second French Plan for Open Science**

> France is committed to ensuring that the results of scientific research are open to all, researchers, companies and citizens, without hindrance, without delay, without payment.[^french-plan]

[^french-plan]: [Second French Plan for Open Science](https://www.ouvrirlascience.fr/deuxieme-plan-national-pour-la-science-ouverte-pnso/)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .center width=40%}
![](images/logo-PNSO2.png){width=60%}
:::
::: {.column width=60%}
**1.** Generalize open access to publications<br>
**2.** Structure, share and open research data<br>
**3.** Open and promote source codes produced by research<br>
**4.** Transforming practices to make open science the default principle<br>
:::
::::

<!-- page -->

## Open Science in France

**The French Open Science Strategy (OSS) 2026–2033**

> The French Open Science Strategy (OSS) 2026–2033, aims to strengthen the transformations initiated with the two previous national plans. Covering eight years, it is structured around ambitions, challenges, strategic objectives, and four-year action plans. The 2026–2029 action plan breaks down 8 strategic objectives into 30 actions and 75 measures.[^OSS]

[^OSS]: [The French Open Science Strategy](https://www.ouvrirlascience.fr/french-open-science-strategy/)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .center width=20%}
![](images/image-OpenScienceStrategy.png){width=80%}
:::
::: {.column width=80%}
OSS Strategic objectives :

**1.**  Encourage a shift in practices to make open science the default approach<br>
**2.** Consolidate the governance and instruments of open science policy<br>
**3.** Reinforce the ecosystem of open science services and infrastructures, pillars of academic sovereignty<br>
**4.** Consolidate france’s position within the european and international open science landscape<br>
**5.** Structure and support open, reliable and high-quality academic publishing<br>
**6.** Consolidate the structuring of open and shared research data in accordance with the FAIR principles<br>
**7.** Increase the openness and valorisation of source code and software from research projects<br>
**8.** Ensure the transparency of clinical trials<br>
:::
::::

# Legal concerns

## Legal concerns

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=80%}
<br />
The Law for a Digital Republic (**_LOI n° 2016-1321 pour une République Numérique (1)_**) is a French law promulgated on October 7, 2016. &nbsp;[{{< fa globe >}}](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFTEXT000033202746)
:::

::: {.column width=10%}
:::

::: {.column width=10%}
![](images/journaux-officiels.jpg)
:::

::::


#### Article 30

> **This article grants authors the right to disseminate their research in open access.**


#### Article 533-4

::: {.small}
- **I.** Lorsqu’un écrit scientifique issu d’une activité de recherche financée au moins pour moitié par des dotations de l’État, des collectivités territoriales ou des établissements publics, par des subventions d’agences de financement nationales ou par des fonds de l’Union européenne est publié dans un périodique paraissant au moins une fois par an, **SON AUTEUR DISPOSE, MÊME APRÈS AVOIR ACCORDÉ DES DROITS EXCLUSIFS À UN ÉDITEUR, DU DROIT DE METTRE À DISPOSITION GRATUITEMENT DANS UN FORMAT OUVERT**, par voie numérique, sous réserve de l’accord des éventuels coauteurs, la **VERSION FINALE DE SON MANUSCRIT ACCEPTÉE POUR PUBLICATION**, dès lors que l’éditeur met lui-même celle ci gratuitement à disposition par voie numérique ou, à défaut, à l’expiration d’un délai courant à compter de la date de la première publication. Ce délai est au **MAXIMUM DE SIX MOIS** pour une publication dans le domaine des sciences, de la technique et de la médecine et de douze mois dans celui des sciences humaines et sociales.
- La version mise à disposition en application du premier alinéa ne peut faire l’objet d’une exploitation dans le cadre d’une activité d’édition à caractère commercial.
- **II.** Dès lors que les **DONNÉES ISSUES D’UNE ACTIVITÉ DE RECHERCHE FINANCÉE AU MOINS POUR MOITIÉ PAR DES DOTATIONS DE L’ÉTAT**, des collectivités territoriales, des établissements publics, des subventions d’agences de financement nationales ou par des fonds de l’Union européenne ne sont pas protégées par un droit spécifique ou une réglementation particulière et qu’elles ont été rendues publiques par le chercheur, l’établissement ou l’organisme de recherche, leur **RÉUTILISATION EST LIBRE**.
- **III.** L’éditeur d’un écrit scientifique mentionné au I ne peut limiter la réutilisation des données de la recherche rendues publiques dans le cadre de sa publication.
- **IV.** Les dispositions du présent article sont d’ordre public et toute clause contraire à celles-ci est réputée non écrite. 
:::

# Ethics : *the FAIR & CARE principles*

![](images/image-FAIR_CARE.png){width=70%}

<!-- page -->

## Ethics : the *FAIR principles*

*A set of guiding principles for managing research data to make it **F**indable, **A**ccessible, **I**nteroperable, and **R**eusable by humans and machines[^wilkinson][^gofair].*<br/>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=25%}
**To be Findable:**

- (meta)data are assigned a globally unique and persistent identifier<br/>
- data are described with rich metadata (defined by R1 below)<br/>
- metadata clearly and explicitly include the identifier of the data it describes<br/>
- (meta)data are registered or indexed in a searchable resource<br/>
:::
::: {.column width=25%}
**To be Accessible:**

- (meta)data are retrievable by their identifier using a standardized communications protocol<br/>
- the protocol is open, free, and universally implementable<br/>
- the protocol allows for an authentication and authorization procedure, where necessary<br/>
- metadata are accessible, even when the data are no longer available<br/>
:::
::: {.column width=25%}
**To be Interoperable:**

- (meta)data use a formal, accessible, shared, and broadly applicable language for knowledge representation.<br/>
- (meta)data use vocabularies that follow FAIR principles<br/>
- (meta)data include qualified references to other (meta)data<br/>
:::
::: {.column width=25%}
**To be Reusable:**

- meta(data) are richly described with a plurality of accurate and relevant attributes<br/>
- (meta)data are released with a clear and accessible data usage license<br/>
- (meta)data are associated with detailed provenance<br/>
- (meta)data meet domain-relevant community standards<br/>
:::
::::


[^wilkinson]: [Wilkinson _et al._ (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18)
[^gofair]: [GO FAIR](https://www.gofair.foundation/)

<!-- page -->

## Ethics : the *CARE principles*

**Definition**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=65%}
>Indigenous data are data, information, and knowledge, in any format, that impact Indigenous Peoples, nations, and communities at the collective and individual levels; data about their resources and environments, data about them as Individuals, and data about them as collectives[^Carroll1],[^Carroll2].<br>

**to go further**

- [GIDA : Global Indigenous Data Alliance](https://www.gida-global.org/) 
- [GBIF : Global Biodiversity Information Facility *Open data for people and purpose: GBIF establishes task group on Indigenous data governance*](https://www.gbif.org/news/1Ke3Gk2USgdIW5OgDlBIKY/open-data-for-people-and-purpose-gbif-establishes-task-group-on-indigenous-data-governance) 
- [GEO : Group on Earth Observation](https://earthobservations.org/groups/geo-indigenous-alliance) 
- [DoraNum](https://doranum.fr/aspects-juridiques-ethiques/les-principes-care_10_13143_af7s-g015/)
:::
::: {.column .center width=35%}
![](images/image-care.png){width=100%}
Source: [Carroll _et al._ (2020)](https://doi.org/10.5334/dsj-2020-043)
:::
::::

[^Carroll1]: [Carroll _et al._ (2020)](https://doi.org/10.5334/dsj-2020-043)
[^Carroll2]: [Carroll _et al._ (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-021-00892-0)

## Ethics : the *CARE principles*

#### **The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=70%}
>The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) was adopted during the fifteenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP 15) [...] Among the Framework’s key elements are 4 goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030.<br>
:::
::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-logo-KMGBF.jpg){width=50%}
:::
::::

#### **Target 21** :Ensure That Knowledge Is Available and Accessible To Guide Biodiversity Action
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=70%}
>Ensure that the best available data, information and knowledge, are accessible to decision makers, practitioners and the public to guide effective and equitable governance, integrated and participatory management of biodiversity, and to strengthen communication, awareness-raising, education, monitoring, research and knowledge management and, also in this context, **traditional knowledge, innovations, practices and technologies of indigenous peoples and local communities** should only be accessed with their free, prior and informed consent[1], in accordance with national legislation[^CBD].<br>
:::
::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-target21.png){width=50%}
:::
::::

[^CBD]: [CBD (2023)](https://www.cbd.int/gbf/targets/21)

## Ethics : The *FAIR & CARE principles*

**Differences and complementarities**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=70%}
>Operationalizing the FAIR Principles for scientific data with the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance enhances machine actionability and brings people and purpose to the fore to resolve Indigenous Peoples’ rights to and interests in their data across the data lifecycle[^Carroll].<br>
:::

# Some Focus

## Focus on the Nagoya protocol

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=60%}

> The **Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization (ABS)** to the Convention on Biological Diversity is a supplementary agreement to the Convention on Biological Diversity. 

> It provides a **transparent legal framework** for the effective implementation of one of the three objectives of the CBD: **the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of the utilization of genetic resources**[^CBD]. 

*The Nagoya Protocol on ABS was adopted on 29 October 2010 in Nagoya, Japan and entered into force on 12 October 2014*.
 
:::
::: {.column .center width=40%}
![](images/image-nagoya.jpg){width=90%}
:::
::::



[^CBD]: [CBD](https://www.cbd.int/abs/about/default.shtml)

<!-- page -->

## Focus on Rare and Threatened Species

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
>The geographic coordinates of species sightings, habitat data, and breeding sites are often vital to conservation efforts, but they can also be misused, especially in the context of poaching and illegal wildlife trade. Researchers and conservationists face a delicate balance between making data openly available for the advancement of science and protecting the species they aim to conserve[^stewart]

>Web-accessible biodiversity databases accept and openly share species observations from the public, benefitting research, conservation, and education. However, public data sharing can also bring harm, for example by facilitating poaching. Databases may mitigate harm by designating certain species as “sensitive” and restricting access to those species data[^Kaehrle].
:::
::: {.column width=50%}
![](images/image-iucn.jpg){width=100% fig-align='center'}
:::
::::

[^stewart]: [Stewart (2025)](https://aquila.usm.edu/smirc/2025/1/5/)
[^Kaehrle]: [Kaehrle & Eschenfelder (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1002/pra2.1259)

## Focus on General Data Protection Regulation - GDPR

**Definition and perimeter**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=70%}

> The acronym **GDPR stands for "General Data Protection Regulation."** The GDPR governs the processing of personal data within the territory of the European Union. <br/>

> **‘personal data’** means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (**‘data subject’**); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a **name**, an **identification number**, **location data**, an **online identifier** or to one or more factors specific to the **physical**, **physiological**, **genetic**, **mental**, **economic**, **cultural** or **social identity** of that natural person[^GDPR][^CNIL].<br/>
:::

::: {.column width=30%}
![](images/image-logo-gdpr.jpg){width=100%}
:::
::::

It **harmonizes rules across Europe** by providing a single legal framework for businesses, enabling them to develop their digital activities within the EU by fostering user trust.

[^CNIL]: [CNIL](https://www.cnil.fr/fr/rgpd-de-quoi-parle-t-on)
[^GDPR]: [GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-4-gdpr/)

## General Data Protection Regulation - GDPR

**Principles**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=40%}
- Principles relating to processing of personal data
- Lawfulness of processing
- Conditions for consent
- Conditions applicable to child's consent in relation to information society services
- Processing of special categories of personal data
- Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences
- Processing which does not require identification
:::
::: {.column width=60%}
![](images/image-gdpr-principles.jpg){width=100%}
[Image from UserCentrics](https://usercentrics.com/knowledge-hub/principles-of-gdpr/)
:::
::::

For more information [GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/) & [CNIL](https://www.cnil.fr/fr/reglement-europeen-protection-donnees)
